title: DOC: fix typo and inconsistencies in RidgeClassifier docstrings
body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

### Describe the issue

In `sklearn/linear_model/_ridge.py`, there are several docstring issues 
in the Ridge classifier classes:

**1. Typo in `_RidgeClassifierMixin.predict`**

Current:
    X : {array-like, spare matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)

Should be:
    X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)

**2. Extra space in `Ridge` See Also section**

Current:
    RidgeClassifierCV :  Ridge classifier with built-in cross validation.

Should be:
    RidgeClassifierCV : Ridge classifier with built-in cross validation.

**3. Missing RST function links in `RidgeClassifier` solver descriptions**

`Ridge` correctly uses RST `:func:` links for solver references:
    'cholesky' uses the standard :func:`scipy.linalg.solve` function
    'sparse_cg' uses :func:`scipy.sparse.linalg.cg`
    'lsqr' uses :func:`scipy.sparse.linalg.lsqr`

But `RidgeClassifier` describes the same solvers as plain text without 
`:func:` links, making the documentation inconsistent.

### Steps to reproduce

Open `sklearn/linear_model/_ridge.py` and search for:
- `spare matrix` in `_RidgeClassifierMixin.predict`
- Double space after colon in the See Also section of `Ridge`
- The solver descriptions in `RidgeClassifier` vs `Ridge`

### Suggested fix

- Fix `spare` → `sparse` in `_RidgeClassifierMixin.predict`
- Remove extra space in See Also section
- Add `:func:` RST links to solver descriptions in `RidgeClassifier`

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

_No response_

title: Documentation: Inconsistent parameter naming in preprocessing modules
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

## Documentation: Inconsistent parameter naming in preprocessing modules

### Introduce yourself
I'm a user of scikit-learn who has been working with machine learning libraries for a while. I've noticed inconsistencies in parameter naming across different preprocessing modules that could be confusing for users.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
There are inconsistencies in parameter naming across different preprocessing modules in scikit-learn. For example, some modules use `random_state` while others use `seed` or `random_seed` for the same functionality. This inconsistency makes it harder for users to remember parameter names and can lead to errors when switching between modules.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce
1. Compare parameter names across different preprocessing modules
2. Look for modules that use `random_state` vs `seed` vs `random_seed`
3. Notice the inconsistency in naming conventions

### Expected Results
Consistent parameter naming across all preprocessing modules. If a parameter is used for randomization, it should consistently be named `random_state` to maintain API consistency.

### Actual Results
Inconsistent parameter naming across modules:
- Some modules use `random_state`
- Some modules use `seed` 
- Some modules use `random_seed`

### Versions
N/A - Documentation issue

### Interest in fixing the bug
I would be interested in working on this documentation improvement if it's accepted.

title: Add a warning whenever `metrics.confusion_matrix` is called with non-numeric values but no labels provided
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Whenever an array-like of string types for a multi-class classification problem is passed into the `confusion_matrix` function without an argument passed for labels, the confusion matrix is returned with the classes in alphabetical order.
While this is expected behaviour and the natural way to sort anything string-like, the outputted confusion matrix may have an output order that is different from the user's expectations, especially if the classes are ordinal. Since the output of the `confusion_matrix` function is an array, without any explicit labels, this means it will need to be manually re-aligned with the labels. 
There is currently no warning for this, possibly leading to misunderstood confusions matrices by users.

### Describe your proposed solution

Near the start of the `confusion_matrix` function, check if the type of the arrays are string-like (or another type without an inherent order) and if `labels` is `None`, i.e. the default value. If this condition is True, raise a warning for the user that their confusion matrix will be returned in alphabetical order.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

There is a valid alternative view that the user should be aware their inputs have no natural order, unless provided, and so should take responsibility for the validity of their inputs. However, this proposed warning would not affect a small number of use cases and would induce a very small computational overhead

### Additional context

_No response_
author: conor-hamill

comments.author: StefanieSenger
comments.body:
Thanks for your suggestion, @conor-hamill.

I can see how that could lead people to mis-interprete their `confusion_matrix`, but nonetheless I would tend to not add a new `Warning` here.

The reason is that in scikit-learn we try to only add warnings if a user likely needs to take action on it (such like in a deprecation) and rely on documentation otherwise. Warnings are barely read and can feel annoying or overwhelming to users, especially if we add to many. 

In this case, we have documented the behaviour:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/b9a147f2d9f3d80d142ed4b02f8d401c140272bf/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py#L454-L455

And a user who is aware of the string label sorting would not need to take any action, so we don't want to force them to pass labels only to suppress a warning.

I will therefore close this issue. Happy to reopen it if other maintainers feel differently about this.

---
Not sure, but is a warning like that maybe an interesting feature for [skore](https://github.com/probabl-ai/skore), @GaetandeCast?

comments.author: GaetandeCast
comments.body:
Yep we have noticed the issue in skore too: https://github.com/probabl-ai/skore/issues/2861 😁 

We have not decided on a solution and a warning may not be what we go for as we are not particularly fond of those either.

Thanks for the heads-up @StefanieSenger !

Looks like we are using deprecated `scipy.stats.mstats.mquantiles` in a number of places:
```

title: Sharing links from scikit-learn.org gives the wrong link
body:
### Introduce yourself

Web Technologies Evangelist for the Safari and WebKit teams at Apple. I'm passing on a report we received about broken functionality on the scikit-learn.org website that was reported to us.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When sharing a link from a page on the scikit-learn.org website, the shared link is incorrectly formatted and loses the `.org` from the host. This is due to `.org` being missing in the OpenGraph URL meta tag:

```
<meta content="https://scikit-learn/stable/auto_examples/datasets/plot_iris_dataset.html" property="og:url"/>
```

Fixing this will fix link sharing.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

1. Load a page on the site: (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/datasets/plot_iris_dataset.html)
2. Share to Messages via the toolbar button
3. Send the link, then copy it and note that the resulting link is missing `.org`

### Expected Results

Sharing a link should result in a valid URL to the site.

### Actual Results

The link shared in the example case is: https://scikit-learn/stable/auto_examples/datasets/plot_iris_dataset.html

### Versions

```shell
# Not Applicable
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

I am passing this issue on for project maintainers to fix.

title: `CalibratedClassifierCV(method="sigmoid")` should always take the raw logits as inputs instead of the predicted probabilities
body: This is a defect [I first observed while reviewing the temperature scaling PR](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31068#discussion_r2012459507): if the uncalibrated classifier only exposes a `decision_function` and no `predict_proba` (which is the case for SVMs for instance) our implementation of sigmoid calibration (aka Platt-scaling) is fine because the output values of `decision_function` are morally logits between -inf and +inf with 0 as the default decision threshold. But if the uncalibrated classifier already exposes a `predict_proba` method (e.g. `GaussianNB`), our current implementation takes the predicted probabilities as input of the parametrized sigmoid function. This is incorrect: we should the log of the probabilistic predictions (incremented by a small epsilon) to feed logits as inputs to the sigmoid function. I had started an unfinished WIP branch now turned into a draft PR (https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34313) to attempt to fix this problem and started to do empirical evaluation to assess the impact of this change in examples. Early results were very promising. However, it would now need work to be sync with main again after the merge of the temperature scaling PR and I got distracted and this was burried in my personal TODO list of WIP stuff to revive. Meanwhile, the following paper by @eugeneberta, @dholzmueller et al. was published, and it confirms that it is empirically much better to take the logits, in which case it is a very competitive calibration method (better than most other calibration methods on average on a large set of data & model pairs). CalArena: A Large-Scale Post-Hoc Calibration Benchmark https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30188 Side note: I suspect that OvR Platt-logits followed by post-hoc class-wise renormalization would also work very well in the multiclass setting, but this does not seem to have been explored in the above paper from a cursory glance. Do you confirm @eugeneberta, @dholzmueller?
author: ogrisel

If you click through to the [interactive flamegraph](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/df8d26b5-5624-4883-a41f-62998c1ad4a0) you'll see `sklearn.utils._encode._unique_python` is 10% of this profile, and most of that time is actually in counting the unique values.

Essentially you stick to Python's `Counter` and do post-processing on that, instead of subclassing and overriding it (cause it has a fast C implementation if you use it directly). I have a sketch that works, and will submit a PR that is less sketchy.

comments.body:
Started writing tests, and also found a bug in the current implementation: if you have multiple different nans (e.g. `NAN = float("nan"); [np.nan, NAN, NAN]`), you get incorrect counts, because for uniqueness purposes they are different, but the counting code merges their counts. So the counts would be `{np.nan: 3, NAN: 3}` in this case, instead of the correct `{np.nan: 1, NAN: 2}`.

In practice this isn't likely to be an issue, because for the common case you only ever get `np.nan` used as an indication of missing data, but technically it can happen.

title: det_curve thresholds docstring claims a decreasing array but returns increasing
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the issue

While reviewing the ranking metrics for a custom evaluation pipeline, I noticed a direct contradiction in `sklearn.metrics.det_curve`. 

The docstring in the file `sklearn/metrics/_ranking.py` mentions that the returned threshold array is 
"Decreasing thresholds on the decision function (either `predict_proba` or `decision_function`) used to compute FPR and FNR."

However, the function actually returns the array in strictly **increasing** order. This contradiction is even visible in the official docstring example for the function.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce
Here is a minimal reproducer proving the array is ascending:
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import det_curve

y_true = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 1])
y_scores = np.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.35, 0.8, 0.9])
fpr, fnr, thresholds = det_curve(y_true, y_scores)

print(f"Thresholds: {thresholds}")
# Output: [0.1  0.35 0.4  0.8  inf]
```

`Scikit-Learn Version: 1.8.0`

### Suggested potential alternative/fix

The fix is pretty straightforward : Update `sklearn/metrics/_ranking.py` to say "Increasing" instead of "Decreasing" for the `thresholds` return value.

Let me know i'll be more than happy to raise a quick PR.

title: DictionaryLearning with split_sign=True breaks Pipeline.predict, get_feature_names_out and float32 dtype preservation
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I am saikrishna working as a senior data engineer I have bachelors degree in computer science with data analytics specialization where I have worked on wide variety of tools like numpy, pandas, scikit-learn,... Where i have done various projects using various tools. Now I was reading the source looking for a bug to fix, part of it while testing a piece of code i have come across this. So i wanted to contribute and help tool perform better.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

so the `split_sign=True` makes `transform` return `2 * n_components` columns and the rest of the class does not know this. A `DictionaryLearning(split_sign=True)` step inside a `Pipeline` fits without any issue initially and then raises at `predict`.

so this has 3 symptoms:
- `get_feature_names_out()` returns half the names
- `set_output(transform="pandas")` raises `Length mismatch`
- float32 input comes back as float64

This also affects all three sparse-coding transformers: `DictionaryLearning`, `MiniBatchDictionaryLearning`, `SparseCoder`.

Previous works: 
- #11000 already has DictionaryLearning and MiniBatchDictionaryLearning checked off as dtype-preserving.

- #32077 brought `SparseCoder` into the common tests and yet the float32 upcast survives in all the three because no common tests sets `split_sign=True`.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import DictionaryLearning
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X = np.random.RandomState(0).rand(60, 5) + 0.5
y = np.random.RandomState(1).rand(60)

dl = DictionaryLearning(n_components=4, split_sign=True, random_state=0).fit(X)
print("n feature names:", len(dl.get_feature_names_out()))
print("n transform columns:", dl.transform(X).shape[1])
print("float32 input -> output dtype:", dl.transform(X.astype(np.float32)).dtype)

pipe = make_pipeline(
    DictionaryLearning(n_components=4, split_sign=True, random_state=0), Ridge()
)
pipe.fit(X, y)
pipe.predict(X)
```


### Expected Results

```
n feature names: 8
n transform columns: 8
float32 input -> output dtype: float32
```
`pipe.predict(X)` returns an array of 60 predictions instead of raising.

The name count must match the transform width, the dtype should be preserved and a fitted pipeline should be able to predict.


### Actual Results

```
n feature names: 4
n transform columns: 8
float32 input -> output dtype: float64

```

yes

so while going through the file i found `sklearn/decomposition/_dict_learning.py:1149-1160`,
`_BaseSparseCoding._inverse_transform`, already accounts for `split_sign`:
```python
expected_n_components = dictionary.shape[0]
if self.split_sign:
    expected_n_components += expected_n_components
```
It expects `2 * n_components` and undoes the split. But `_n_features_out` in the same
file returns the unsplit count in all three classes:
- `SparseCoder` line 1412
- `DictionaryLearning` line 1750
- `MiniBatchDictionaryLearning` line 2334

**root cause**
1. those three `_n_features_out` properties
2. `_BaseSparseCoding._transform` allocates the split array as
   `np.empty((n_samples, 2 * n_features))`, no `dtype=`, so always float64
3. `DictionaryLearning.fit_transform` returns the raw code `V` and never applies the
   split (the other two classes have no `fit_transform` override, so they are fine here)

The reason its not caught yet is that `split_sign=True` has exactly one test in the suite,
`test_dict_learning_split` in `sklearn/decomposition/tests/test_dict_learning.py`, and it
only exercises `transform` and `inverse_transform` and no common test sets `split_sign=True`.

fix can be, make `_n_features_out` account for `split_sign` in all three,
allocate the split array with the input dtype, and have `fit_transform` apply the same
split `transform` does.

Thanks for the detailed report. I dug into this and confirmed all three symptoms:

title: Inconsistent `_check_initialized` method: only present on gradient boosting estimators
body:
While reviewing #34495, I noticed that `_check_initialized` only exists on the gradient boosting estimators and nowhere else in the codebase. The method does nothing but wrap `check_is_fitted(self)`.

## Steps to reproduce
```
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    AdaBoostClassifier,
    GradientBoostingClassifier,
    GradientBoostingRegressor,
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    RandomForestClassifier,
)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

estimators = [
    GradientBoostingClassifier(),
    GradientBoostingRegressor(),
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier(),
    AdaBoostClassifier(),
    RandomForestClassifier(),
    LogisticRegression(),
]

for est in estimators:
    print(f"{type(est).__name__:32s} _check_initialized? {hasattr(est, '_check_initialized')}")
```

## Results
```
GradientBoostingClassifier       _check_initialized? True
GradientBoostingRegressor        _check_initialized? True
HistGradientBoostingClassifier   _check_initialized? False
AdaBoostClassifier               _check_initialized? False
RandomForestClassifier           _check_initialized? False
LogisticRegression               _check_initialized? False
```

## Background
I tried to trace how the method was introduced. As far as I can tell it first appeared in 2015 and was never explicitly discussed — the surrounding conversations are all about the apply method. Please correct me if I've missed something:
- 2015: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/5228
- 2016: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/7464
- 2019: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/14545

## Questions
1. Should `_check_initialized` be generalized across the other estimators — e.g. moved up into `BaseEnsemble`?
2. Or should it be removed, since it's a redundant wrapper around `check_is_fitted` and inconsistent with the rest of the codebase?
author: iivko

comments.author: StefanieSenger
comments.body:
I think we can simply remove `_check_initialized` and replace it by `check_is_fitted`, @iivko.
It looks like a historical leftover to me.

Cleanups are always very welcome! Happy to review you PR.

`BaseGradientBoosting._raw_predict` currently calls `check_is_fitted` twice and maybe we can clean this up in the same PR.

comments.author: lesteve
comments.body:
So it does seem like a variation of the cython 3.2.6 regression https://github.com/cython/cython/issues/7767 with a `pickle` `dumps/loads` roundtrip on top of it? cc @da-woods for expert advice on whether this can be considered a Cython bug or not (it kind of seems like one).

I created a minimal reproducer in https://github.com/lesteve/scikit-learn-34525-cython-reproducer.


My understanding is that using `functools.update_wrapper` on a Cython function will fail the `pickle` `dumps/loads` roundtrip with the confusing error `AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute '__annotate__'`.

Here is an example closer to the scikit-learn code:

```py
import pickle
from functools import update_wrapper

import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import KDTree


class Wrapper:
    def __init__(self, function):
        self.function = function
        # if you remove the next line this works
        update_wrapper(self, function)

    def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        return self.function(*args, **kwargs)


tree = KDTree(np.zeros((2, 2)))
wrapped = Wrapper(tree.query)

payload = pickle.dumps(wrapped)
# The next line yields AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute '__annotate__'
pickle.loads(payload)
```

comments.author: da-woods
comments.body:
Thanks for the report. I agree it's probably a bug. It isn't immediately obvious to me how to fix it but will think about it some more.

(The problem isn't so much how to fix it, as how to fix it minimally)

comments.body: I've just created a Cython issue for now.

comments.author: da-woods
comments.body: I've now fixed this in Cython. I'm not sure when the next release is likely to be, but it'll be in that.

title: MAINT - Remove Sass dependency
body:
Replace `sphinxcontrib-sass` with plain CSS files using native CSS nesting, which is now supported by all modern browsers. The SCSS files used minimal Sass features — mostly nesting, comments, and a single mixin.

To show how I would do it, please see POC: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34413 - the css edits are done. 
~~Before I fix the CI errors it would be great to hear from people.~~ 
EDIT: The CI is green

As a reference: 
https://tech-insider.org/sass-vs-css-2026/#:~:text=Expert%20Opinions%3A%20Fireship%2C%20ThePrimeagen%2C%20Kevin%20Powell%2C%20Adam%20Argyle

@scikit-learn/core-devs
author: DeaMariaLeon

comments.author: betatim
comments.body:
I don't have a strong opinion on this and also not a lot of experience with modern CSS development.

Having looked at the POC PR my impression is that to make the switch we mostly just change how comments are made.

If this is all we need to do to remove a dependency and the associated complexity then I am 👍

comments.author: thomasjpfan
comments.body: As long as we are okay with not supporting browsers older than Dec 2023, then we can use CSS nesting: https://caniuse.com/css-nesting

comments.author: Charlie-XIAO
comments.body: I'm personally +1 for this. Since the website is mainly developer-facing, requiring a browser feature 3 years ago does not sound too bad. Moreover our styling was mostly an additional layer on top of pydata-sphinx-theme, so even without any of our CSS, most contents are still readable. sphinxcontrib-sass is not a very actively maintained dependency, and not relying on a postprocessor also cuts off some boilerplates.

comments.author: GaelVaroquaux
comments.body:
> requiring a browser feature 3 years ago does not sound too bad.

I'm slightly worried about that. Do we have data on what fraction of browsers are more than 3 years old?

comments.author: Charlie-XIAO
comments.body:
As of June 2026, among the top 10 browsers in https://www.w3counter.com/globalstats.php, <10% are on chrome <120.

*Note that <10% among top 10 doesn't mean <10% among all though, as the top 10 only sum up to slightly over 50%.*

Not sure but I think the main affected users are probably not "normal users who forgot to update for a few weeks", but maybe those on old Android/WebView stacks, or old OS images, or environments where browser updates are intentionally pinned. But as said even in those cases, basic content readability will not be affected that much.

comments.author: betatim
comments.body: You can configure https://caniuse.com/css-nesting to show you support weighted by browser usage. It can also show you support by region (or country) (top right of the screenshot). The main "not supported" browser seems to be an older version of Chrome (~3% globally, more popular in Europe and South America). I think this is fine. But, what would be nice is to use the website with CSS nesting disabled and experience myself what it is like. Does someone know how I could do that in my modern Firefox? (I'd rather not mess around trying to install an old version of Chrome).

comments.author: betatim
comments.body: n.b. canisue.com allows you to upload usage data from your own analytics, so we could get another view for scikit-learn.org users. I stopped exploring this option when plausible wasn't listed as a source. If someone has experience/motivation to find out if we could use our plausible data that could be another bit of data to base this decision on.

comments.author: GaelVaroquaux
comments.body:
In my experience, typical situations where users are stuck with old software is in large corporations or institutions where policies hold back software updates.

Those people matter because they are typically industry users of scikit-learn with real business impact and/or can be high-level decision makers. It would be a pity if they have a hard time reading the docs.

comments.author: betatim
comments.body:
I agree with the idea and hence often vote for supporting age old versions of our dependencies. From what I can tell though, the versions of Chrome (4 to 108) are very old. Google does not offer a "long term support" like Microsoft did for IE at some point (meaning there were lots of legitimate users with an otherwise considered insecure browser). This makes me think that these users are not in an institution/corporation. I could imagine that it is people who own a laptop that is quite old and has stopped receiving OS updates (I can see two such macbooks from where I sit ...). As a result of the lack of OS updates these people might be stuck with old browsers.

I put AI to work to find some data sources that would give some insight on this. The only public dataset it came up with are stats from wikimedia. In particular `all_sites_by_os_and_browser_percent.tsv` from https://analytics.wikimedia.org/published/datasets/periodic/reports/metrics/browser/. About 50% of all traffic is Chrome (any version). 2.5% is from Chrome < 108. Of these "old chromes" 50% are Windows and 37% macos. An interesting finding is that ~60% of these "old chrome on windows" users look like they are on Windows 10. This means they should be auto updating to a modern Chrome version. Windows 7 users seem to be stuck on Chrome 108 (21%).

Similarly the largest part of "old chrome on macos" users are on a modern version of macos, so should be updating.

An explanation that the AI offered for this conundrum (why don't they update?) is that these might be scripts/bots that have a hardcoded user agent. I don't know what to make of that, it is an interesting idea. But I think "users stuck on old OS via corporate policy" is just as good an explanation (and maybe more plausible?).

---

In firefox you can go to `about:config` and then search for `layout.css.nesting.enabled` and disable it. Then visit the rendered docs from the POC PR https://output.circle-artifacts.com/output/job/82065fe7-ca2b-46c6-86a1-f48a56100e2a/artifacts/0/doc/_changed.html. This gives people an impression of what our website would feel like for those effected.

comments.author: betatim
comments.body:
Apparently the landing page and the testimonials page are the ones that make most use of CSS nesting. I have to admit that I have a hard time seeing a difference :-/ Either disabling nesting with the above recipe doesn't work or I am not paying enough attention?

If I ask AI what should break it lists for example the gradient by the logo on the landing page. If I manually remove this then the page looks ugly but you can still read everything (light mode). In dark mode the bullet points become essentially invisible.

My conclusion is that the actual impact seems small/negligible for those users who are using a browser that doesn't support CSS nesting.

Maybe someone who actually understands browser and CSS could post a screenshot of a "with nesting support" and "without nesting support" browser?


TL;DR: I still vote to use nesting and removing a dependency that isn't super actively maintained.

comments.author: GaelVaroquaux
comments.body:
> I have to admit that I have a hard time seeing a difference :-/

Well that settles the debate. Thank you Tim!

+1 for moving on

comments.author: DeaMariaLeon

Opera Mini: 2015

comments.author: betatim

> BTW: showing information only on `hover` goes against "accessibility rules". We have lots of that.

Ahrg! While it isn't great that we have these problems, I am super happy that as a project we are in a place where we can and do try and make progress on this! comments.author: DeaMariaLeon
comments.body:
Regarding the security risks using old browsers: Huge companies have to comply with industry standards and are periodically audited. 

If an audit finds a fleet of outdated browsers, that's a finding the company has to remediate — and it can affect certifications, customer contracts, and cyber-insurance. 

A company must get "ISO certified number xyz". The "xyz" depends on the type of industry. 

Example of a standard: https://www.iso.org/standard/75652.html

title: Backport workflow-hardening fix (excessive-permissions) to 4 release branches
body:
### Summary The default branch already hardened `.github/workflows/cuda-ci.yml`, `.github/workflows/update-lock-files.yml`, `.github/workflows/wheels.yml` against the issue(s) below, but **4** release branches still carry it. title: Infinite Recursion when using a mock as param for a Mock Classifier
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

For verifying the behaviour of our code, we create a mock classifier that is passed down to the functions to train and optimize our model. In scikit-learn 1.9.0, this creates an infinite recursion, and in case of a heavier mock classifier a memory leak.

The code to reproduce the issue is below. A larger example can be found in this gist: https://gist.github.com/phyk/666b7ef4cabf0becff18bea9d13e9389

For both snippets, you need to run them using pytest to get the behavior.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from unittest.mock import MagicMock

from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, ClassifierMixin, clone


class FastMockClassifier(BaseEstimator, ClassifierMixin):
    def __init__(self, learning_rate: float = 0.1) -> None:
        self.learning_rate = learning_rate


def test_clone_recursion_leak() -> None:
    clone(FastMockClassifier(learning_rate=MagicMock()))
```

### Expected Results

Under scikit-learn 1.8, this test just passes.

### Actual Results

Under scikit-learn 1.9, this snippet uses an unproportionate amount of memory and time. 

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, would be available for fixing it.
author: phyk

comments.author: TONGSUOregonState
comments.body:
I was able to reproduce this on the current main branch (`1.10.dev0`).

The recursion is triggered in `_clone_parametrized` when accessing
`estimator._metadata_request`. Since the estimator parameter is a
`MagicMock`, accessing that missing attribute dynamically creates another
`MagicMock`, which is then cloned again:

```text
MagicMock
→ MagicMock._metadata_request
→ MagicMock._metadata_request._metadata_request
→ ...
```

As an initial experiment, I avoided the recursion by checking the estimator's
instance dictionary with:

```python
vars(estimator)["_metadata_request"]
```

This made the reproducer pass and preserved the behavior covered by the
metadata-routing regression tests.

However, `vars(estimator)` only checks the instance `__dict__`. It could miss
a legitimate `_metadata_request` provided through `__slots__`, a class
attribute, or a descriptor.

A more general candidate approach is therefore to use
`inspect.getattr_static(estimator, "_metadata_request")` to check whether the
attribute actually exists without invoking `MagicMock.__getattr__`. If the
static lookup succeeds, the code can then access and clone the real
`_metadata_request` as before.

Candidate diff:

```diff
 try:
-    new_object._metadata_request = clone(estimator._metadata_request)
+    inspect.getattr_static(estimator, "_metadata_request")
 except AttributeError:
     pass
+else:
+    new_object._metadata_request = clone(estimator._metadata_request)
```

This keeps the clone-based behavior introduced in #33827, so the metadata
routing owner is not deep-copied, while avoiding dynamically generated mock
attributes.

Tests run with the candidate change:

- `sklearn/tests/test_base.py`: 104 passed, 6 skipped
- `sklearn/tests/test_metadata_routing.py`: 100 passed
- Issue reproducer: passed

I have not opened a PR because the issue is still marked `Needs Triage`. I can
open one once the approach is confirmed.

comments.author: StefanieSenger
comments.body:
I will close this issue as out of scope. The failure comes from putting a `MagicMock` object into a constructor param (`learning_rate`, which actually expects float), then clone the estimator. This is not how users are supposed to use scikit-learn.

Happy to reopen in case I misunderstood and there is a real use case, @phyk.

title: Consider switching to pyrefly for typechecking
body:
I'd like to propose adding [Pyrefly](https://pyrefly.org) for typechecking - it could either be added alongside mypy as a non-blocking CI check or migrated entirely. Happy to open the PR, checking here first to see if there's interest?

For transparency I work on the Pyrefly team, I've been looking into the performance of mypy vs Pyrefly on real repos and when I tried out sklearn the results looked promising enough that I thought I'd share :)

I did some initial investigation, running locally mypy 2.3.0 vs Pyrefly 1.1.1 (checking `sklearn/`) which shows Pyrefly is ~29x faster:

  | Checker   | Run        |
  |-----------|------------|
  | mypy      | **18.4 s** |
  | Pyrefly   | **0.6 s**  |


## How to make the switch:

  1. **Add the dependency** to the test/lint requirements: `pyrefly>=1.1.1`.
  2. **Add `[tool.pyrefly]` config** mirroring the existing `[tool.mypy]` config.
     ```toml
     [tool.pyrefly]
     project-includes = ["sklearn"]                        # matches `mypy sklearn/` in build_tools/linting.sh
     search-path = ["."]
     project-excludes = ["**/sklearn/externals*"]          # mirrors mypy's exclude
     preset = "legacy"                                      # matches mypy's non-strict defaults
     ignore-missing-imports = ["joblib.*", "sklearn.externals.*", "*"]  # mirrors ignore_missing_imports + follow_imports=skip
     ```
  3. **resolve/suppress error code differences** There are some differences between the errors pyrefly catches and what mypy does (79 new errors from what I can see running locally, details below), so we could either ignore them  (`# pyrefly: ignore [code]`) for now or see if there are genuine issues to address. If we opt for removing mypy we could also remove ~80 out of 82 mypy ignores that pyrefly doesn't complain about, so the total ignores would stay roughly the same.
  4. **Setup in CI** in .github/workflows/lint.yml (`build_tools/linting.sh`), mirroring the mypy
     step with a run pyrefly check step.

## Error differences - Mypy vs Pyrefly

  When I compared pyrefly and mypy output, I found 79 new errors from Pyrefly that aren't flagged by Mypy. Some might be real typing issues that should be resolved, but I'm not super familiar with the sklearn codebase so would require some deeper investigation. Here's a summary of the differences:

  | Error code | Count | Reason for difference | Suggested approach |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `bad-override` | 72 | Estimator subclasses override base `fit`/`transform`/callback methods with looser signatures than Pyrefly's LSP-override check allows — 54 in `sklearn/` (mostly `cluster/*`), 18 in tests. Pyright/mypy are more permissive here. | Suppress - looks mostly benign; could align a few signatures over time |
  | `missing-attribute` | 3 | `pytest` narrowed to `None` via the optional-import guard in `estimator_checks.py` (`.mark`/`.param`) | Suppress |
  | `bad-argument-type` | 1 | `_openml.py:716` | **Review** and consider fixing |
  | `no-matching-overload` | 1 | `_metadata_requests.py:1668` | **Review** and consider fixing|
  | `unsupported-operation` | 1 | `instance_generator.py:1356` | **Review** and consider fixing|
  | `missing-argument` | 1 | `estimator_checks.py:956` | **Review** and consider fixing|
  | **Total** | **79** | | **~75 suppress · ~4 review** |
author: javabster

title: PytestRemovedIn10Warning (pytest version 9.1.1.) with sklearn parametrize_with_checks
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

The recent pytest update (9.1.1) introduces a warning in our scikit-learn compatibility tests for our own encoders. Our encoder inherits from scikit-learn’s `TransformerMixin` and `BaseEstimator`, and we use `sklearn.utils.estimator_checks.parametrize_with_checks` to verify that the custom encoders are compatible with scikit-learn.

The warning originates from `parametrize_with_checks`, which essentially returns a `pytest.mark.parametrize`. It currently passes a generator to `pytest.mark.parametrize`. However, this is deprecated in current versions of pytest.

It would therefore be useful to review or update the `parametrize_with_checks` implementation so that it no longer relies on the deprecated generator behavior. This will allow us in the future to keep testing for scikit-learn compatibility.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Run the following file using pytest's latest version (9.1.1):

```python
import pytest
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.utils.estimator_checks import parametrize_with_checks


@parametrize_with_checks([DummyRegressor()])
def test(estimator, check):
    check(estimator)
```

This can be run from terminal with `pytest name_of_file.py`


### Expected Results

The expected result is no warning about deprecation from pytest.

### Actual Results

```
PytestRemovedIn10Warning: Passing a non-Collection iterable to parametrize is deprecated.
Test: LOCATION, argvalues type: generator
Please convert to a list or tuple.
See https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/deprecations.html#parametrize-iterators
metafunc.parametrize(*marker.args, **marker.kwargs, _param_mark=marker)
```


### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.14.5 (tags/v3.14.5:5607950, May 10 2026, 10:43:50) [MSC v.1944 64 bit (AMD64)]
executable: LOCATION\python.exe
   machine: Windows-11

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.0
          pip: 26.2.1
   setuptools: None
        numpy: 2.5.1
        scipy: 1.17.0
       Cython: None
       pandas: 3.0.2
   matplotlib: 3.10.9
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
     narwhals: 2.22.1

Built with OpenMP: True

threadpoolctl info:
       user_api: openmp
   internal_api: openmp
    num_threads: 4
         prefix: vcomp
       filepath:LOCATION\site-packages\sklearn\.libs\vcomp140.dll
        version: None

       user_api: blas
   internal_api: openblas
    num_threads: 4
         prefix: libscipy_openblas
       filepath: LOCATION\site-packages\numpy.libs\libscipy_openblas64_-b788215d9d47792bcba3a2e2a7114320.dll
        version: 0.3.33.112.0
threading_layer: pthreads
   architecture: SkylakeX

       user_api: blas
   internal_api: openblas
    num_threads: 4
         prefix: libscipy_openblas
       filepath: LOCATION\site-packages\scipy.libs\libscipy_openblas-64eda39e79589aedb16f58e5547eb599.dll
        version: 0.3.30
threading_layer: pthreads
   architecture: SkylakeX
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The fix seems relatively easy.
The link in the warning provides a solution: https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/deprecations.html#parametrize-iterators

As such, we could wrap the return generator in a list like:

```python
return pytest.mark.parametrize(
        "estimator, check",
        list(_checks_generator(estimators, legacy, expected_failed_checks)),
        ids=_get_check_estimator_ids,
    )
```

comments.author: SparshGarg999
comments.body:
### Proposed Plan to Resolve Pytest 9 Deprecation Warning in `parametrize_with_checks`

Passing non-collection generators to `pytest.mark.parametrize` raises `PytestRemovedIn10Warning` in Pytest 9.1.1+.

**Fix:**
Wrap generator return objects in `list(...)` in `sklearn/utils/estimator_checks.py` inside `parametrize_with_checks` before passing to `pytest.mark.parametrize`.

comments.author: lesteve
comments.body: Thanks @cfauchereau for your input! I double-checked and indeed this has already been fixed in `main` in #34448.

comments.author: jameslamb
comments.body:
I'm glad there was a fix quickly applied, but I suspect that once a `pytest` 10.x comes out changing this warning to an error, it might cause problems for projects that try to stay compatible with a wide range of `scikit-learn` versions (since the fix will presumably only be in the next version, `>1.9.0`).

In case it's helpful to anyone finding this issue from search in the future... here's how we're attempting to maintain backwards and forwards compatibility with both `scikit-learn` and `pytest` in LightGBM's tests:

```python
from sklearn.utils.estimator_checks import parametrize_with_checks as sklearn_parametrize_with_checks


def parametrize_with_checks(estimator, *args, **kwargs):
    mark_decorator = sklearn_parametrize_with_checks(estimator, *args, **kwargs)
    argnames, argvalues = mark_decorator.args
    return pytest.mark.parametrize(argnames, list(argvalues), **mark_decorator.kwargs)

@parametrize_with_checks(
    [lgb.LGBMClassifier(), lgb.LGBMRegressor()],
    expected_failed_checks=_get_expected_failed_tests,
)
def test_sklearn_integration(estimator, check):
    estimator.set_params(min_child_samples=1, min_data_in_bin=1)
    check(estimator)
```

ref: https://github.com/lightgbm-org/LightGBM/pull/7407

title: [DOC] Improve docstring for `orthogonal_mp`
body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

Currently, the [rendered documentation for `linear_model.orthogonal_mp`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.orthogonal_mp.html#sklearn.linear_model.orthogonal_mp) ([source](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/cc50648cc1b759b53a4edbce0f3bb6c237349448/sklearn/linear_model/_omp.py#L316-L324)) is missing a formalism and the included LaTeX is not rendered. 

Further, looking at the included formalisms, it seems that the notation is changed between this docstring and [the User Guide section on Orthogonal Matching Pursuit](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html#orthogonal-matching-pursuit-omp), which uses a _w_ rather than a _gamma_.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

I see two potential fixes:

1.  Updating the docstring formatting and notation. I would suggest standardizing this with what's currently in the User Guide :

```
    Solves `n_targets` Orthogonal Matching Pursuit problems.
    Each instance of the problem aims to approximate the optimum solution vector, parametrized by the number of non-zero coefficients using
    `n_nonzero_coefs`:

    .. math::
        \underset{w}{\operatorname{arg\,min\,}}  ||y - Xw||^2_2 \text{subject to} ||w||_0 <= n_{nonzero coefs}

    When parametrized by error using the parameter `tol`:

    .. math::
        \underset{w}{\operatorname{arg\,min\,}}  ||w||_0 \text{subject to} ||y - Xw||^2_2 <= tol
```

2. Removing this portion of the docstring to direct users towards the formalism in the User Guide, as is done for `linear_model.OrthogonalMatchingPursuit`.

I'm happy to open a PR with either fix !

> * This is expected because the lint lock-file is actually from the PR branch (we use `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` on purpose). The motivation for this IIRC is to give the linting error lines as they are in the contributor editor.

I also think this is on purpose. It is useful if you update the version of the linter (or change the linter) so you can see what the result is of doing that. So I would keep it as is.

> * it looks like `lint.yml` is from `main` since the line that fails tries to get the `pyrefly` version. Probably in a `pull_request` worfklow the workflow yaml is from the merge of `main` into the PR branch?

This is how it should be IMHO. Both the fact that `pull_request` uses the workflow from `main` and that we want it to do that. If we used the workflow from the PR branch you'd have lots of PRs that are green but will then fail once merged into `main` due to linter mismatches. And I think the fact that `pull_request` uses the workflow from `main` is a security thing.

I like the comment you added to the `checkout` workflow. I tend to forget how exactly GitHub combines my branch with `main` to run the tests, etc. So this is a nice comment to have.

title: Inconsistent type of predictions and `classes_` for array API classifiers
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

There's currently 2 classifiers with array API support:
* `LogisticRegression`
* `RidgeClassifier`

The docs and discussions in this issue tracker are quite unclear about what should be the expected behavior when input types are mixed in the case of classifiers.

Since in general 'y' can be something like strings or non-sequential integers that get re-encoded internally, I think it makes sense that the `classes_` attributes under array API would be obtained from the type of 'y' and then sliced when returning something from `.predict()` - i.e. "prediction follows 'y'".

This appears to be the case for `LogisticRegression`:
```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

import numpy as np
import torch

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.random(size=(20,3))
y = rng.integers(2, size=X.shape[0])
yt = torch.tensor(y, device="xpu", dtype=torch.float32)

from sklearn import set_config
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)
model = LogisticRegression(solver="lbfgs").fit(X, yt)
model.classes_
```
```
tensor([0., 1.], device='xpu:0')
```

But the docs state "everything follows 'X'" instead, and `RidgeClassifier` does appear to follow this logic from the docs, even if it might not be as natural for classification scenarios:
```python
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeClassifier
model = RidgeClassifier(solver="svd").fit(X, yt)
model.classes_
```
```
array([0., 1.], dtype=float32)
```

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Described above.

### Expected Results

All classifiers with array API support should work like in `LogisticRegression`.

### Actual Results

`RidgeClassifier` works differently.

title: Support infinite values in DecisionTree/RandomForest/ExtraTrees (now that NaN is supported)
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Hello,

I am facing a problem where the proper handling of infinite values would be helpful. Since the introduction of the support for missing values (#23595/#26391/#27966), I was wondering to what extent it would be possible to handle those.

Currently:

```
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [np.inf], [10.0]])
y = [0, 0, 1, 1]
DecisionTreeClassifier().fit(X, y)
# ValueError: Input X contains infinity or a value too large for dtype('float32').
```

This is because infinite value is explicitly rejected regardless, in `BaseDecisionTree._compute_missing_values_in_feature_mask` (`sklearn/tree/_classes.py`):
A second guard in `_validate_X_predict` (same file) does the same at predict time.

```
if not np.isfinite(overall_sum):
    # Raise a ValueError in case of the presence of an infinite element.
    _assert_all_finite_element_wise(X, xp=np, allow_nan=True, **common_kwargs)
```

Both guards live on `BaseDecisionTree`, shared by all four tree classes; `RandomForest*`/`ExtraTrees*` call the same method rather than duplicating it. 

`GradientBoostingClassifier`/`Regressor` don't set `allow_nan` and aren't affected either way. Small number of call sites.

### Describe your proposed solution

The splitter already tolerates infinite values without modification. Unlike NaN, +inf/-inf are ordinary totally-ordered floats (-inf < finite < +inf), so <= comparisons already place them correctly, with no new split-evaluation logic needed like NaN required. Verified by monkeypatching out just the two guards: DecisionTreeClassifier fits and predicts correctly on +inf/-inf data, including placing a real split threshold at -inf. Checked sklearn/tree/_splitter.pyx too: thresholds are computed as feature_values[p_prev]/2.0 + feature_values[p]/2.0 (sum-of-halves, to avoid overflow on large finite values), with a fallback to feature_values[p_prev] if the result lands exactly on +INFINITY/-INFINITY. With real -inf in the data this fallback is a no-op (-inf sorts first, so the fallback value is -inf too).

check_estimators_nan_inf (the common test for this) is already skipped entirely for these estimators (gated by one allow_nan tag covering both NaN and inf), so relaxing the guard doesn't remove existing coverage, though new tests would need to be added for inf specifically. Proposal: relax the two guards (behind allow_nan or a new dedicated tag), and add that dedicated inf/NaN test coverage.

title: Pandas output path fails to reject infinite values during transform
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When using `set_output(transform="pandas")`, `SelectKBest.transform` does not reject infinite values in a pandas `DataFrame`. This is a regression introduced by [PR #25102](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/25102).

The pandas-output path passes `cast_to_ndarray=False` to `_validate_data`, which causes `check_array` to skip its `force_all_finite` validation. This allows invalid numeric inputs through `transform` instead of raising the expected validation error.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif

X_train = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "a": [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0],
        "b": [1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 2.0],
    }
)
y = [0, 0, 1, 1]

selector = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=1).set_output(transform="pandas")
selector.fit(X_train, y)

X_bad = X_train.copy()
X_bad.loc[0, "a"] = np.inf

print("Input containing infinity:")
print(X_bad)
print()

try:
    result = selector.transform(X_bad)
    print("Transform succeeded (no error raised):")
    print(result)
except Exception as exc:
    print("Error:", exc)
```

### Expected Results

The input containing infinity should be rejected during `transform`:

```
Input containing infinity:
     a    b
0  inf  1.0
1  1.0  2.0
2  0.0  1.0
3  1.0  2.0

Error: Input X contains infinity or a value too large for dtype('float64').
```

(This is the behavior when `set_output` is not used.)

### Actual Results

No validation error is raised; transform silently succeeds:

```
Input containing infinity:
     a    b
0  inf  1.0
1  1.0  2.0
2  0.0  1.0
3  1.0  2.0

Transform succeeded (no error raised):
     b
0  1.0
1  2.0
2  1.0
3  2.0
```

### Versions

```
scikit-learn 1.9.0
Python 3.11.13
Linux
NumPy 2.4.6
SciPy 1.17.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The pandas-output path should preserve DataFrame containers without changing the estimator's validation behavior. Infinite values should continue to be rejected consistently during `transform` regardless of the output format setting.

title: [UX] display more informative ellapsed time info in progress bar output for short tasks
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

Once fit tasks are completed, the progress bars display `0:00:00` for tasks that last less than a second, which is quite common in practice. I think we should display milliseconds and maybe drop the leading `0:` for hours, since we almost never do fit tasks that last hours (at least in interactive shells and notebooks where progress bars are most useful).

More concretely, if a fit task last 10 ms, we could display `0:00:00.010` or `00:00.010` for instance.

The full traceback is in the details below. I put AI to work to figure this out, it started as trying to understand a failure in the cuml CI. The "cause" for the failure in CI is that we started using Python 3.14.7. AI dug around for a while and found https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/150024 and the following reasoning about what is happening. > Two threads touch the same list: > > - `ScoringMonitor.__init__` registers its own `append` as a message consumer, `open_listener(self._log.append, owner=self)` (`sklearn/callback/_scoring_monitor.py:124`), so `_log` grows as scores arrive. > - The estimator carrying that monitor in `_skl_callbacks` is pickled to the workers by loky's queue-feeder **thread** (`loky/backend/queues.py:159`). title: Array API: Ridge with alpha as an array fails due to misconfigured checks
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When trying to fit a ridge model with the array API on multi target objective, if one want to pass an array for alpha, the checks are not well configured I think, leading to an impossibility.
Here is a small reproducer.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

import torch

from sklearn import config_context
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression

title: Interactions between array API and sparse coefficients are not documented
body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

Array API support was recently expanded to cover LogisticRegression, which allows having sparse coefficients:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/9eff0fd241a2c2221112d0f7461876208e6b05d4/sklearn/linear_model/_base.py#L508

It's not expected that coefficients would have exact zeros with the supported solver 'lbfgs' for array API (although it can still happen when columns have the same value in all rows), but technically a user can still call `.sparsify()` on an estimator that was fitted to array API classes, in which case it will fail.

The documentation is not clear about limitations of LogisticRegression under array API, such as not being able to sparsify coefficients or not being able to make predictions if it somehow succeeds.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Documentation should be clear about limitations of methods from estimators when using array API classes.

title: DOC: fix grammatical errors in AdaBoostClassifier and AdaBoostRegressor docstrings
body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

### Describe the issue

In `sklearn/ensemble/_weight_boosting.py`, there are several grammatical 
errors and inconsistencies in the docstrings of `AdaBoostClassifier` 
and `AdaBoostRegressor`:

**1. Missing word in module docstring**

Current:
    This module structure is the following:

Should be:
    The module structure is as follows:

**2. Grammar error in `decision_function` and `staged_decision_function`**

Current (appears multiple times):
    Binary classification is a special cases with ``k == 1``

Should be:
    Binary classification is a special case with ``k == 1``

**3. Grammar error in `staged_decision_function`, `staged_predict_proba`**

Current (appears multiple times):
    The order of outputs is the same of that of the :term:`classes_` attribute.

Should be:
    The order of outputs is the same as that of the :term:`classes_` attribute.

**4. Grammar error in reference citation in `AdaBoostRegressor`**

Current:
    An AdaBoost [1] regressor

Should be:
    An AdaBoost [1]_ regressor

Note: `AdaBoostClassifier` correctly uses `[1]_` with the trailing 
underscore for RST citation syntax, but `AdaBoostRegressor` is missing it.

### Steps to reproduce

Open `sklearn/ensemble/_weight_boosting.py` and search for the phrases above.

### Suggested fix

Fix the grammatical errors and citation syntax as described above.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

_No response_

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body: I marked this issue as a bug but I don't know if it's a bug in scikit-learn, loky or scipy.

comments.author: imann128
comments.body: When using joblib with the loky backend for parallel queries, shared arrays get memory mapped as read only buffers. Cython's auto-generated setters for cdef public const attributes (idx array, node_data, node_bounds) reject read only buffers, which is another open issue tracked by a TODO. Previous work done regarding this issue was done in `#5639` but that was a partial fix. To fix this, I am thinking about updating __setstate__ to copy the read-only arrays before assignment.

comments.author: betatim
comments.body: xref https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34409

comments.author: betatim
comments.body: AI suggests that a change to cython that was fixed in https://github.com/cython/cython/pull/7768 is the reason for the `__annotate__` errors. This means that updating to cython 3.2.8 is the fix (3.2.7 was released and yanked because the wrong commit was tagged).

comments.author: imann128
comments.body:
Is there a manual pin that needs bumping to Cython ≥3.2.7, or will this resolve once pylatest_pip_scipy_dev picks it up automatically? 
Also, after going through cython/cython#7768 this looks the plausible fix. My PR was targeting a symptom, not the actual bug.
Thanks for tracing it down.

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body: Cytnon 3.2.8 should be online: https://github.com/conda-forge/cython-feedstock/pull/194

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body: Actually, this is running against 3.3.0a2.dev0 which should also contain the fix but apparently that's not the case...

comments.author: ogrisel
comments.body:
I checked and Cython 3.3.0a2.dev0 was update this morning as expected: https://anaconda.org/channels/scientific-python-nightly-wheels/packages/Cython/overview ...

Maybe the fix is not enough?

comments.author: lesteve
comments.body:
Minor note: Cython is built from source in the scipy-dev build, i.e. it does not rely on scientific-python-nightly-wheels upload (which can lag a bit behind Cython source sometimes). We do:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/d1f1734eca972396774aff4be157bfbcac971236/build_tools/github/install.sh#L82

I am wondering, whether it's not an old bug reported in cloudpickle that resurfaced in a new Python 3.14 minor release [^1] https://github.com/cloudpipe/cloudpickle/issues/585? Somebody created a PR a few weeks ago https://github.com/cloudpipe/cloudpickle/pull/594, not sure if that's a reasonable approach and I won't have the bandwidth to look into it more.

[^1]: likely Python 3.14.6 that was released June 10 according to [this](https://peps.python.org/pep-0745/#bugfix-releases)

comments.author: imann128
comments.body: It was a cython compiler bug. In the meantime, it can be fixed by adding a upper bound to the cython version if that helps.

title: PowerTransformer raises raw TypeError on Pandas nullable integer (Int64) and float (Float64) dtypes containing pd.NA
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When passing a Pandas `DataFrame` containing modern nullable extension dtypes (such as `Int64` or `Float64`) with missing values (`pd.NA`) into `PowerTransformer`, the estimator crashes with an unhandled internal exception (`TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous`) rather than coercing the array cleanly or raising a standard scikit-learn `ValueError`.

### Context & User-Facing Impact

1. **Modern Pandas Integration:** With modern Pandas workflows (including Pandas 2.0+ defaults and `df.convert_dtypes()`), nullable integer and float types are standard when working with tabular data that contains missing values. 
2. **Pipeline Failures:** In production data pipelines, passing a DataFrame with nullable dtypes directly into a scikit-learn `Pipeline([('power_transform', PowerTransformer()), ...])` causes the entire pipeline to fail with a low-level Pandas boolean evaluation error instead of processing the data smoothly.
3. **Unnecessary Workarounds:** To bypass this bug, users currently have to manually write boilerplate pre-casting logic (e.g., `df.astype("float64")`) before calling `PowerTransformer`, which breaks scikit-learn's native DataFrame compatibility goals.
4. **Consistency:** Most scikit-learn estimators handle Pandas extension arrays seamlessly by converting them to standard floating-point NumPy arrays via `_validate_data`. `PowerTransformer` should follow this same pattern.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer

# Minimal DataFrame using Pandas nullable integer extension dtype ('Int64')
# The missing value (None) is automatically represented as pd.NA
X = pd.DataFrame({"col": pd.Series([1, 2, None, 4], dtype="Int64")})

# Triggers raw TypeError inside PowerTransformer during internal array checks
pt = PowerTransformer(method="box-cox")
pt.fit_transform(X)
```

### Expected Results

`PowerTransformer` should automatically coerce Pandas nullable extension arrays into standard IEEE floating-point NumPy arrays (`np.float64` or `np.float32`) via `_validate_data` before evaluating numerical bound checks.

Specifically:
- It should not crash with a raw `TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous`.
- Passing data with nullable dtypes should either complete successfully (coercing `pd.NA` to `np.nan`) or raise a clear, standardized `ValueError` if input constraints are violated.

### Actual Results

The estimator crashes with a raw `TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous` during internal positivity checks (`X <= 0`):

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "reproduce_bug.py", line 9, in <module>
    pt.fit_transform(X)
  File "sklearn/base.py", line 1478, in fit_transform
    return self.fit(X, **fit_params).transform(X)
  File "sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py", line 3218, in fit
    return self._fit(X, y, force_transform=False)
  File "sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py", line 3232, in _fit
    if np.any(X <= 0):
  File "pandas/core/ops/common.py", line 81, in new_method
    return method(self, other)
TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.12.3
executable: /usr/bin/python3
   machine: Linux-6.8.0-generic-x86_64

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.0
        numpy: 2.5.1
        scipy: 1.18.0
       pandas: 3.0.4
   matplotlib: 3.9.0
       joblib: 1.4.2
threadpoolctl: 3.5.0
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I am interested in opening a Pull Request to fix this issue once it has been triaged!

### Root Cause Analysis

In `PowerTransformer._fit` (inside `sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py`), positivity and finite bounds checks—such as `np.any(X <= 0)`—are executed on the input `X` **before** array validation occurs:

```python
# Current order of execution in _fit():
if np.any(X <= 0):  # <--- Fails here on Pandas ExtensionArrays containing pd.NA
    raise ValueError(...)

X = self._validate_data(X, ...)
author: Dikshant-Neupane

comments.author: virchan
comments.body:
Thank you for reporting this issue, @Dikshant-Neupane, and for helping to improve scikit-learn.

I cannot reproduce the reported error using the provided reproducer:

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer

X = pd.DataFrame({"col": pd.Series([1, 2, None, 4], dtype="Int64")})

pt = PowerTransformer(method="box-cox")
print(f"{pt.fit_transform(X) = }")
# array([[-1.22474379e+00],
#        [-2.15713130e-06],
#        [            nan],
#        [ 1.22474595e+00]])
```

<details>

<summary>Python Dependencies</summary>

```bash
      sklearn: 1.10.dev0
          pip: 26.1.2
   setuptools: 82.0.1
        numpy: 2.5.1
        scipy: 1.18.0
       Cython: 3.2.9
       pandas: 3.0.5
   matplotlib: 3.10.8
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
     narwhals: 2.24.0
```

comments.author: Dikshant-Neupane
comments.body:
Hi @virchan, thanks for looking into this.

You are correct that the reproducer completes successfully on the main branch.

After further investigation, the issue was specific to an older version of scikit-learn. In the older version, the positivity check (np.any(X <= 0)) was executed before array validation. This caused pd.NA in Pandas ExtensionArrays to trigger the TypeError before it could be coerced.

In the current main branch, the logic has already been refactored (inside _check_input). validate_data is now called first, correctly converting pd.NA into standard np.nan before the numerical bounds check (np.nanmin(X) <= 0) is performed.

Since this is already resolved on main, feel free to close this issue.

comments.body:
Finding the real best categorical split for abs error is really hard, a computationally tractable way was found only recently: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08470 (experiment code: https://github.com/Stargazer-cyk/binary-split)

We should **first quickly go for 1 or 2 (to fix the CI flakiness)**, and then maybe consider implementing this paper. But while this paper is fun and all, I'm not sure it's worth the effort:
- I'm pretty sure the currently implemented approach, while not always producing exact best splits, produces overall similarly good trees.
- I looked into the experiment code, and I find the way the comparison with lightGBM is presented in the paper a bit misleading... 

That said the speed is super appealing, I'm investigated a bit to understand where it comes from.

comments.body:
If I'm not mistaken, to have this huge speed up, they need the column to be sorted. That's why they sort features in the code and benchmark them separately, I guess, LGBM just does not get faster (or that much faster) if the data is sorted.
I'm not sure, how it will work on real dataset with arbitrary large number of rows and categorical features, with different orderings for different features.

title: radius_neighbors with array radius works with n_jobs=1 but raises ValueError for n_jobs>1
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When `radius` is passed as a per-sample array, `NearestNeighbors.radius_neighbors` returns a correct result with `n_jobs=1` but raises a `ValueError` with `n_jobs>1` on identical input for both `ball_tree` and `kd_tree`. An `n_jobs` value should not change behavior.

`NearestNeighbors` is a convenient interface to `BallTree` and `KDTree` because, unlike those, it accepts an `n_jobs` parameter.

I used the following workaround in the past, [here](https://github.com/nicolassalvy/ClippedDensityCoverage/blob/main/ClippedDensityCoverage/metrics/Clipped_Density_Coverage.py#L52-71):
```python
tree = NearestNeighbors(
    algorithm="ball_tree", n_jobs=n_jobs
).fit(data1)

distances, indices = (
    tree.radius_neighbors(
        X=data2,
        radius=np.max(radii),
        return_distance=True,
        sort_results=False,
    )
)

correct_indices = [
    indices[i][distances[i] <= radii[i]]
    for i in range(len(distances))
]
```
but this can be very slow, both because of the mandatory `return_distance=True` and because of the following: adaptive radius search is useful here because the typical distances in different data modes can be very different, one mode where they are very far apart and another where they are close. With the workaround, the indices returned for half the data could be that whole half every time, which makes the results very slow.

A related feature request showed interest: [#25970](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/25970) ("Allow NearestNeighbor radius_neighbors to accept an array for the `radius` keyword argument"), though this present issue is only about the tree-based algorithms, which already accept it at `n_jobs=1` and only break under parallelism, not the `brute`-force case.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I'm Daniel and I use Scikit-learn both in private projects and at work. I work as a Data Scientist and currently building a personal project.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

So I am working on a data classification project and trying to use one-hot encoding within a pipeline.  I have organised my columns based on the needed impute through SimpleImputer (mean and most frequent). Simple imputer was able to impute where its needed and ignore non-missing columns but One-Hot always encode everything regardless of dtype. And I couldn't avoid that without re-editing my columns even though my groupings work well without repetition. 

### Describe your proposed solution

My proposed solution is to add a `skip` kwarg so the user can select the columns to skip during the process. I believe better solutions could be developed but thats what I am currently thinking.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Could probably use `make_column_selector` but the user still has to manually encode at some point.

### Additional context

_No response_

comments.author: cakedev0
comments.body:
Hi, thank you for the report.

At first glance, it feels like `ColumnTransformer(..., remainder=True)` and `make_column_selector` should let you do what you want.

Can you add a bit more details? Ideally some code example with a small toy dataset.

comments.body:
> import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

> data = pd.DataFrame({
>     "age": [20.0, np.nan, 40.0, 30.0],
>     "visits": [1, 2, 1, 2],  
>     "city": ["London", np.nan, "Paris", "London"],
> })
> 
> imputer = ColumnTransformer(
>     [
>         ("mean", SimpleImputer(strategy="mean"), ["age", "visits"]),
>         ("mode", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent"), ["city"]),
>     ],
> )

> process = Pipeline([
>     ("impute", imputer),
>     ("encode", OneHotEncoder()),
> ])
> 
> result = process.fit_transform(data)
> print(process.get_feature_names_out().tolist())


This results are:

`['mean__age_20.0', 'mean__age_30.0', 'mean__age_40.0', 'mean__visits_1.0', 'mean__visits_2.0', 'mode__city_London', 'mode__city_Paris']`


Now pipeline did the whole dummy encoding irrespective of the dytpe which means it would create a spill of numerical variables that should otherwise not be encoded within the pipeline. Therefore the skip protocol would allow the user to skip the some columns within the pipelines that they dont want affected. I have gone through the docs of the one hot encoder

Also I could use `column_selector` like you suggested but that would remove the simplicity of a pipeline.
with the skip *kwargs , i would be:

`Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(
        strategy="most_frequent"
    ),
    ("encode", OneHotEncoder(
        skip=["age", "income"]
    )),
])`

comments.author: cakedev0
comments.body:
Thanks for the example — this is expected: once `ColumnTransformer` stacks its output, a plain `OneHotEncoder()` downstream has no notion of "which columns are categorical" anymore, it just sees an array and encodes every column. So this isn't really about `OneHotEncoder` needing a `skip` param — it's that the encoding step should live *inside* the `ColumnTransformer`, next to the imputation, not after it:

```python
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer, make_column_selector
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

categorical = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("encode", OneHotEncoder()),
])

preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", SimpleImputer(strategy="mean"), make_column_selector(dtype_include="number")),
    ("cat", categorical, make_column_selector(dtype_exclude="number")),
])
```

This gives you exactly what you want (numeric columns imputed only, categorical columns imputed + encoded) without adding column-selection logic to `OneHotEncoder` itself — that's what `ColumnTransformer` is for. Adding a `skip`/column-selection kwarg to every transformer would duplicate that responsibility across the codebase, so I'd lean toward closing this as "works as intended" / documentation gap rather than an API change. Happy to reconsider if there's a scenario `ColumnTransformer` genuinely can't cover.

title: PCA does not follow same namespace checking logic as others
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

In most array API estimator methods that happen after `.fit()`, if an incompatible input is passed to the method, it throws an informative error message, usually coming from `check_same_namespace` - for example:
```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(100,10))
y = rng.standard_normal(size=X.shape[0])

import dpnp
Xd = dpnp.array(X, device="gpu")

from sklearn import set_config
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
Ridge(solver="svd").fit(Xd, y).predict(X)
```
```
ValueError: Inputs passed to Ridge.predict() must use the same namespace and the same device as those passed to fit(). Array namespaces used during fit (dpnp) and predict (sklearn.externals.array_api_compat.numpy) differ. You can move the estimator to the same namespace and device as X with: 'from sklearn.utils._array_api import move_estimator_to; xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(X); estimator = move_estimator_to(estimator, xp, device)'
```

The error type in this case is `ValueError`.

But PCA's methods like inverse_transform do not use that utility function, erroring out with a less informative message instead, and with the error type being `TypeError`:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/bb9df11710fc918df3110565b5145b8247c0ab47/sklearn/decomposition/_base.py#L193

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(100,10))

import dpnp
Xd = dpnp.array(X, device="gpu")

from sklearn import set_config
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
PCA().fit(Xd).inverse_transform(X)
```

### Expected Results

`ValueError` with a similar message as the one thrown by Ridge.

### Actual Results

```
TypeError: Multiple namespaces for array inputs
```

### Versions

```shell
Not relevant.
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

No.
author: david-cortes-intel

comments.author: ajayraj30002
comments.body:
Hi @david-cortes-intel , I was looking into this and would love to help patch it if the team decides to move forward!

It looks like `PCA.inverse_transform` (and likely `PCA.transform`) in `sklearn/decomposition/_base.py` are calling `get_namespace(X, self.components_, ...)` directly, which triggers the generic `TypeError`. 

To align with estimators like `Ridge` and `LogisticRegression`, I can patch these methods to explicitly use the namespace validation utility first:

```python
check_same_namespace(X, self, attribute="components_", method="inverse_transform")
xp, _ = get_namespace(X)
```
Let me know if you'd like me to open a PR for this once triage is complete and the label is updated

comments.author: StefanieSenger
comments.body:
Thanks for reporting, @david-cortes-intel, and for looking into this, @ajayraj30002.

We're currently in the process of fixing all the issues with arrays coming from different namespaces and the while designing a common way how do deal with this. @lucyleeow is mainly working on this, for instance recently in #33525.

Now with `check_same_namespace`, I can see it was introduced rather recently and is used only in discriminant_analysis and linear models, not sure why it is not more broadly used and what the plans are. You can open a PR with your proposed fix, @ajayraj30002, but it may be that there are other plans already.

comments.author: ajayraj30002
lucyleeow
comments.body:
Thanks. To clarify, #33525 addresses a different but seemingly similar issue.

#33525 is about allowing different namespace array inputs to a single method.

`check_same_namespace` is about checking that the namespace used in `fit` is the same as the one used for `predict` (or `transform`).
